job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Yara Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my mum and little brother in a two-bed flat on Fenner Road, and I take the train to Wexcombe University for a master's in cybersecurity. I wake at six, check a few security news feeds, then spend the day in lectures and a lab where we attack and defend practice networks. After my computer science degree I did six weeks in a bank's security operations team, watching alerts. Evenings I do bug-hunting contests on my laptop and sometimes win small prizes. My debt is about 32,000 and my savings are almost nothing, but I pay a share of the rent at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a better autocomplete and I'm happy with it. I use it every day, so I know where it's strong and where it makes things up. I'd post that on the security forum I use, and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it doesn't change my problem, which is that I live in a town with perhaps two security jobs a year. The bank where I interned took one junior last year, and 200 people applied. I'd still be hunting for remote work and entry roles, and carrying the same debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep entering bug contests and aim for two certificates, the kind employers actually filter on. I'd apply to about 60 jobs, mostly remote, and treat every contest as a line on my CV. I'd also keep paying my share of rent at home, 200 a month, because Mum counts on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. A bit restless, because I'd rather be moving than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your bug-hunting look like if AI stayed ordinary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd win a few more prizes, maybe 300 or 400 a month if I'm lucky, and some months nothing at all. It's good CV material, which matters more than the money. A bounty on a real company's site looks better than any exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your plan for jobs in a town with so few?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Remote roles with companies overseas, and any security team in the three biggest cities within a train ride. I'd go to a meetup there every month and try to meet people, since a referral beats a hundred applications.

say: I'd say it's a **better autocomplete** and I'm happy with it, then get on with it.
I'd post on the security forum that the **hype** was louder than the change.
think: It doesn't change my real problem: about **two security jobs** a year in my town.
The bank took one junior and **200 people** applied.
do: Finish the master's and aim for **two certificates** employers filter on.
Apply to **60 jobs**, mostly remote, and keep entering bug contests.
feel: **Okay but restless**, wanting to move rather than wait.
S0.quote: A bounty on a real company's site looks better than any exam.
fieldNote: Yara is **adaptive** and busy, but the scarcity of local jobs keeps her anxious in a flat world.
Bug bounties are both income and CV material.
She pays 200 a month of rent at home, so her mum depends on her.

steps.text: Apply to 60 security jobs, mostly remote, by the end of spring
Enter one bug bounty contest a month for prize money and CV credit
Finish the master's and pay 200 a month toward rent at home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, and I'd say it creates new work as well. AI helps attackers too, so defenders need to be more skilled, not fewer. I'd tell my cohort to stop treating AI as an enemy and start treating it as a colleague that makes mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the entry-level job I did in my six weeks is the first thing to go. Watching alerts, sorting false alarms from real ones, writing up incident notes. An AI does that quickly and doesn't get tired. So the first rung of my own field is exactly what's being cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I'm doing, only faster and more openly. I'd build a small project that uses an AI model to sort alerts, put it on my page and try to show I can manage the tool, not just do the task. I'd also keep hunting bugs, which needs creativity machines don't have yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert. A bit nervous and a bit excited. I like fast-moving things, but I'd like some money behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of an entry security job would the AI take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert triage, which means sorting out which warnings matter. Log reading, writing the summary of an incident. At the bank, a senior analyst named Imogen said half the junior day was that, and the rest was learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that mean for how you'd spend this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend it building one strong thing I can show. And I'd email five managers I met at meetups, to ask what they'd hire for in a world like this. I'd rather ask directly than guess.

say: I'd say AI helps attackers too, so defenders need to be **more skilled, not fewer**.
I'd tell my cohort to treat AI as a **colleague that makes mistakes**.
think: The entry job I did, **watching alerts**, is the first thing to go.
The first rung of my own field is exactly what's being cut.
do: Build a small project that uses an AI model to **sort alerts** and put it online.
Email **five managers** from meetups to ask what they would hire for.
S1.quote: The entry-level job I did in my six weeks is the first thing to go.
fieldNote: Yara sees AI cutting the **junior** rung while raising demand for skilled defenders.
She chooses to show she can manage the tool, not do the task.
Asking managers directly is her typical shortcut.

steps.text: Build an AI alert-sorting project and put it on my portfolio page
Keep entering bug bounty contests for income and credibility
Email five security managers from meetups to ask what they hire for

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to talk about it now, and I'd say it publicly. I'd also say we shouldn't panic. People who panic make bad choices, and I'd rather people hear a calm voice with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel more exposed than I let on. A security job is a thinking job, and AGI does thinking work. I'd have 32,000 of debt in a field whose entry level has been scooped up. But security might be one of the last places people stay, because someone has to be accountable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the master's if a job came, and finish it if not. I'd chase any security work in 90 days, including contract or part-time, and apply to some sort of government or company programme that says it's hiring people for the new world. I'd keep bug hunting, and pick up a trade skill from my uncle, who fits alarm systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a bit giddy, which is odd. I'd feel like I'm part of history, but the bills still come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you spend the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't worry, that I'm working on it, and that I'd keep paying the 200 a month for rent. My brother is 15 and I want him to keep studying. I'd want him to hear it from me, not from the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your mum and brother to know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A month to land three interviews, and a month to figure out what the safest path is. I'd also open a savings account and put in everything I could, even 20 a week. Not a plan, a habit.

say: I'd say **talk about it now**, in public, with a calm voice and a plan.
I'd say people who panic **make bad choices**.
think: A security job is a **thinking job**, and AGI does thinking work.
Security may be one of the last places people stay, because someone must be **accountable**.
do: Chase **any security work** in 90 days, including contract or part-time.
Pick up a **trade skill** from my uncle, who fits alarm systems.
feel: **Anxious**, a bit giddy, part of history while the bills still come.
S2.quote: Security might be one of the last places people stay, because someone has to be accountable.
fieldNote: Yara is the **calmest voice** at two years, yet admits she feels more exposed than she lets on.
She hedges with a trade skill from her uncle, who fits alarm systems.
Her brother is 15 and she wants him to keep studying.

steps.text: Apply for contract and part-time security work within 90 days
Learn alarm system fitting from my uncle on weekends
Put 20 a week into a separate savings account
Keep paying 200 a month so my brother can stay in school

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the real window. I'd talk to anyone who'd listen about getting retraining and income support set up now. Five years is enough if people start. Not enough if they wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to get a real job, build skills and be in a team that handles accountability. I'd expect to still have a place at 2031, since security has people in charge of risk. It's not safe, but it's workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job in the first six months, anywhere decent. I'd study for a serious certificate, put away 250 a month and pay half the debt by year four. I'd also want to move toward governance and risk, the part of security where a person has to sign off and take the blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More hopeful than with two. A bit like being given a map after being dropped in the woods.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the first job, even a lower one. A first job is the entry ticket. After that I can move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first of those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cutting my teeth in a team. I'd ask to be on incident response, where I'd learn the most, even if it's stressful. I'd write a short guide for new juniors, which is useful and also looks good.

say: I'd say five years is **enough if people start** and not enough if they wait.
I'd push for retraining and income support now.
think: Five years is enough to get a **real job** and join a team that handles accountability.
do: Land a **first job** within six months and save 250 a month.
Move toward **governance and risk**, where a person has to sign off.
feel: **More hopeful**, like being given a map after being dropped in the woods.
S3.quote: I'd also want to move toward governance and risk, the part of security where a person has to sign off and take the blame.
fieldNote: With five years Yara sees a **workable** route through accountability roles.

Her target is to halve the debt by year four.

steps.text: Land a first security job within six months of finishing
Save 250 a month and halve the loan by year four
Study for a governance and risk certificate in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long runway and we should use it well. I'd say learn how to work with the tools, since that's the safest thing. I'd tell my younger brother to keep an open mind about what job he'll end up doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel fairly good. In ten years I could be a senior in a security team, even lead one. The tools would do a lot of what juniors do now, but I'd be the one deciding what to trust. The debt would be gone and I might be paying a mortgage by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first job, grow into incident response, and by 28 try to lead a small team. I'd also start a side business doing security checks for small companies, since they can't afford a full team. And I'd save toward a flat. I'd keep paying for my brother's studies for as long as needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, even. It sounds like a good time to be in my field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you aim for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Burnout, maybe. Security is stressful and the pace could be punishing. And a few small worries, like whether people trust the machines too much and stop checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people that a long runway is a gift. If more people knew about it, fewer people would panic.

say: I'd say it's a **long runway** and we should learn to work with the tools.
I'd tell my brother to keep an open mind about his future job.
think: In ten years I could be a **senior** or even lead a team, deciding what to trust.
The debt would be gone and I might be paying a **mortgage**.
do: Take a first job, grow into **incident response** and aim to lead a small team by 28.
Start a **side business** doing security checks for small firms.
feel: **Calm**, even pleased, since it sounds like a good time to be in my field.
S4.quote: A long runway is a gift. If more people knew about it, fewer people would panic.
fieldNote: Yara is **calm** only here: she expects her field to value her judgement and the debt to clear.
Her worry is burnout and people trusting machines too much.
She plans to keep paying for her brother's studies.

steps.text: Take the first security job and move into incident response

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The one with two years. It gives me no time and puts the household's income at risk. What would help is wage support during retraining, a clear line on who is accountable for AI decisions, and employers asked to hire and train juniors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just say that I'm cautious about the idea that people like me are fine because we're adaptable. Being adaptable helps me move fast, but there are only so many seats. I wish someone would say that out loud.

headlineQuote: Being adaptable helps me move fast, but there are only so many seats. I wish someone would say that out loud.
portrait: Yara is 24, doing a **cybersecurity master's** after computer science, with 32,000 of debt and almost no savings.
She lives with her mum and 15-year-old brother, pays 200 a month toward rent, and wins small bug bounties.
She is centrist, **uses AI every day**, and moves fast, building projects and asking managers directly.
Her moods are anxious in most worlds and calm only with ten years, when she expects a senior role.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which gives no time and puts the household's income at risk.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **wage support** during retraining, clear accountability for AI decisions and employers who train juniors.
